content.text:
I judged 19 claims in the document. All are supported by the record, and I flagged none.

- **Cause:** The record backs the change of the cache port from 6379 to 6380 (D1, P2). It also backs the refused connections on 6380 (Gd3f7) and the page working the spend figure out from scratch when the cache can't be reached (S1).
- **"Every lookup failed":** This was the closest call. The log line gives the failures as 50 to 200 of every 200 lookups, with 200 the usual figure, so at least one minute had only 50. I accepted it because the 50 was most likely the partial minute of 03:42. The deploy landed at 03:42:44, so only the last 16 seconds of that minute ran the new revision. If you read "every" more strictly, this is the one claim to look at again.
- **Impact:** The median-latency series rose from about 27 ms to about 190 ms. The error rate stayed within its normal range, which supports "slow but not failing".
- **Ruled-out causes:** The earlier deploy sat inside the 360 minutes of metrics that were read, with the service healthy until 03:43. The diff lists only the values file, so no source code changed.
- **Contributing factors:** The record holds no pre-deploy check, no rollout gate and no cache-failure alert. Connection-refused errors appear from 03:42, before the onset. The alert rule's 5-minute wait is the record's figure. I didn't judge the "had it been otherwise" sentences, since they say what would have happened.
- **"Nobody was paged":** This matches the record's own finding.

I left the action items and verdicts out, as the instructions say.

supported.quote: The production values file had `cache.port` changed from {D1.1} to {D1.2}, and the summary cache refused connections on that port.
Every summary-cache lookup failed, so on every request the account page fell back to working out each shopper's spend figure from scratch.
That fallback keeps pages correct but slow.
A configuration change gave the shop a cache address that refused its connections, so every account page had to be worked out from scratch: the pages stayed correct but got slow.
The refused cache port, or another wrong cache address, could reach production again and slow every account page.
Shoppers' account pages loaded slowly: the slowest replica's median time to answer a request rose far above its usual level, while failed requests stayed within their normal range.

Pages were slow because the account page could not use its rendered-summary cache. Its configuration says that when the cache cannot be reached, the page works out the shopper's spend figure from scratch, and the logs show that happening on every request.

The cache could not be used because every lookup was refused: the service connected to the cache on port {S1.3}, and the cache refused the connection. As read at {T14.1}, all replicas ran revision 0d8e826, whose configuration sets that port.

The service pointed at that port because the deploy of revision 0d8e826 at {P2.1} changed the cache port in deploy/values-production.yaml from {D1.1} to {D1.2}, a port on which the cache refused connections.
The earlier deploy of revision 544cef3 at {P1.1}: the metrics read show the service healthy with it in place until the onset at {began}.
A source-code change shipped in the same deploy: the diff lists only deploy/values-production.yaml, so every other file was as it was at the previous revision.

supported.quote: No check was seen, in review or before the deploy, that the cache address in the deployment configuration accepts connections from the target environment. A change to the cache port shipped to production unchallenged.
The deploy reached every replica, and no gate was seen that watches latency or cache-lookup failures after rollout to halt or reverse it.
No alert on summary-cache lookup failures was seen.
The fault was found only by the latency alert, although connection-refused errors were logged from the first minute.
could have fired sooner than a latency rule that waits {rule_waits} with its condition holding.
Nobody was paged: the HighLatency alert on io-shop was linked to no on-call incident.
